items.title: Diamond does not conduct — graphite does
items.claim: Both diamond and graphite are pure carbon. Diamond is an insulator; graphite conducts electricity along its sheets. Same element, same atoms — wildly different electrical behaviour.

options.text: Graphite is impure and the impurities carry charge

Each carbon in graphite is sp2 with one p-electron contributed to a delocalised pi system spread across the entire sheet — these electrons are mobile and conduct, while diamond's sp3 carbons keep every electron locked in sigma bonds
Graphite ionises into C+ and C- pairs

items.reveal:
Diamond: every carbon is sp3, with four single bonds to neighbours. All valence electrons are in localised sigma bonds. No mobile carriers. Band gap is about 5.5 eV — diamond is an excellent insulator, almost transparent to visible light.

Graphite: each carbon is sp2. Three sigma bonds in the plane, one p-orbital perpendicular. Those p-orbitals overlap across the whole sheet, forming continuous pi bands. The bands are half-filled, like a 2D metal.

Graphene (a single graphite sheet) was isolated by Geim and Novoselov in 2004 and won them the 2010 Nobel Prize. Its electrons behave like effectively massless particles — a result of the band structure.
items.why: Element identity is taught as the main determinant of properties. Structure and bonding can change everything for the same atom.

items.title: More than 99 percent of the visible universe is in a state not taught at GCSE
items.claim: Solid, liquid, gas — the three states of matter on the syllabus. But more than 99 percent of normal matter in the universe (stars, ionised interstellar medium) is plasma — a hot ionised gas with free electrons and ions.
items.prompt: What makes plasma a separate state of matter from a hot gas?

options.text: Plasma is denser than a gas
In plasma the atoms have been ionised so electrons and ions move independently; the substance conducts electricity, responds strongly to electric and magnetic fields, and emits its own light
Plasma is hotter only in name
Plasma is gas that has been compressed

items.reveal:
Heat any gas above a few thousand kelvin and electrons start to break free from atoms. The collection of free electrons and ions is a plasma. Stars, lightning, neon signs, fluorescent lamps and the auroras are all plasmas.

Because charges are free, plasmas have collective behaviours that gases lack: they conduct electricity, they pinch and twist under their own magnetic fields, they support waves that no gas can carry. Magnetohydrodynamics is the whole branch of physics that deals with their flow.

Fusion energy research (ITER, JET, tokamaks) depends on confining hydrogen plasma at over 100 million K with magnetic fields. The plasma cannot touch any wall — the wall would vaporise long before the plasma cooled.
items.why: The 'three states' are good for Earth-surface chemistry. Cosmically, plasma is the default.

items.title: Mendeleev predicted germanium 15 years before anyone made it
items.claim: In 1871 Mendeleev published predicted properties for an undiscovered element he called 'eka-silicon'. In 1886 Winkler isolated germanium. The predicted atomic mass was 72; measured 72.6. Predicted density 5.5 g/cm3; measured 5.32.
items.prompt: How could Mendeleev predict an unknown element?

options.text: He used patterns in the existing table: rows and columns of known elements bracketed each gap. An element in the silicon column, between gallium and arsenic, must have intermediate properties — and atomic mass close to the average of its neighbours
He had advance information from chemists in Germany

items.reveal:
Mendeleev's 1871 predicted properties for eka-silicon: atomic mass ~72, density ~5.5 g/cm3, grey metal, oxide formula MO2 with density ~4.7 g/cm3, chloride MCl4 boiling under 100°C.

Winkler's 1886 germanium: atomic mass 72.6, density 5.32 g/cm3, grey metal, GeO2 density 4.7 g/cm3, GeCl4 boiling at 86°C.

The match converted scepticism into acceptance. The periodic table stopped being a memorisation aid and became a predictive theory. Similar predictions held for gallium (eka-aluminium, 1875) and scandium (eka-boron, 1879).

The predictions could not have worked if the table were merely an empirical classification. The fact that it predicted real properties of unknown elements showed that something deeper was being captured.
items.why: Theories earn their keep by predicting what no one has measured yet. Mendeleev's table did this three times in 17 years.
